source_text: With regard to M-landscape-positioning, I was thinking, Alinery and Mastra are probably the two projects that are most worth doing a deep dive on.  Alinery is "a little bit like" what I'm doing with the design pattern cascades, insofar as it produces graphs that govern workflows and I similarly am creating graphs (or semilattices / CT diagrams) that act as "policies" that regulate workflows.  It's kind of the same thing with a different terminological paint job, but what's interesting about this is not just the similarity but the fact that I didn't see that many other people talking about similar things, whereas much of SF Tech Week was samey-samey.  As for Mastra, it is YC backed and very snazzy, but at least a lot of it is open source and it looks like they are solving some of the same problems as the War Machine, albeit in a different way.  So, my overall sense is that I have been coming at similar problems to SF folks, but with a much more theory-heavy approach (Category Theory & Active Inference) and that I want to be able to demonstrate what's good about my approach while learning from theirs.

reply_text:
Joe, I've cloned Alinery and Mastra into `~/code/external/` and am starting a separate deep dive on each, both running in the background.I'll start by surveying the Alinery clone and the existing landscape entries.Now the scheduler, which determines whether it's a list or a graph.Important: the graph is inferred from artifact path overlap, with SCCs for loops. Let me read the rest of the scheduler logic.The scheduler is a real dataflow engine with provenance, loops and fan-out/fan-in. Let me see the rest and the whitepaper, which may be their theory.I'll start by mapping the Mastra monorepo and the FUTON sources in parallel.Their whitepaper is a formal model where states grow by union, which bears directly on the semilattice question. Reading on.Now a real playbook, the design guidance, and the meta-playbook.I've started both deep dives. Each one is a separate agent reading the code in the background. Neither installs or builds anything, and nothing they write gets committed until I've read it.

- **Alinery vs the pattern cascades** goes to `landscape/deep-alinery.md`. It's checking whether a playbook is really a graph (branches, joins, loops) or just a list of steps. It's also checking whether playbooks can be combined, refined or checked against each other, and whether anything there does the job of a semilattice join. That tells us where "the same thing with a different terminological paint job" holds and where it stops. It's also separating the parts of FUTON that exist in code from the parts that only exist in notes.
- **Mastra vs the War Machine** goes to `landscape/deep-mastra.md`. It compares Mastra's workflows, suspend/resume, memory, scorers, tracing and agent networks with the War Machine. The War Machine side covers dispatch, budget, park and calibration, plus futon1b and minus40. It's also looking at what Mastra keeps in its paid `ee/` directories, which shows what they think is worth charging for. It only reads War Machine files and changes none.

Each write-up ends with **2–4 small demonstrations** where your Category Theory / Active Inference approach should show something the other side can't. Each one has an input, a procedure and a failure condition, and at least one case where the other project is expected to win. That's the "demonstrate what's good about my approach while learning from theirs" part.

I've added your message to the mission as **§6 Deep dives**. The tension "samey vs starred" now records the reason you gave for starring Mastra. I also found a July note, `~/code/TN-deep-research-landscape-position-2026-07.md`, which set aside a separate study of where pattern-cascade learning sits among agent and developer tools. The Alinery dive is a first instalment on that.

I'll report back when both write-ups are in.
